I remember writing in cursive, in elementary school, and it is still a skill which I use intermittently to this day. Sometimes, it makes me feel good knowing that I am probably the only one around who can read/write in cursive... almost like I'm "better" than everyone else, somehow.

Personally, I feel (tinfoil hat time) as if it's going to ultimately separate the working force: those who can and those who can't read/write in cursive. Business will be conducted in cursive, and those that can read/write in it will take part in that business. Those who can't will be relegated to more labor-intensive jobs.

Human history has been littered with this dividing factor, of certain skills and traits separating the working class from the leading class, and with the dying of cursive in schools, I think this will be the new deciding factor. Public schools are slowing the instruction of cursive, until it simply "dies" out... but private schools will continue to teach it as a form of discipline. Those with private school degrees will be more prone to attend prestigious colleges and subsequently get better jobs, and they will know how to write/read in cursive.

It'll almost become a status symbol, as not everyone can use it, and only the most "prestigious" people will. Similarly to how being multilingual is -- if you can fluently converse with your Japanese business partner without a translator, that partner will be more amicable with you -- if you can write to each other and understand each others handwriting, you'll have something in common with each other.

Maybe a novelty, maybe even a status symbol but I have a hard time seeing it ever becoming a practical enough skill to become a real dividing factor unless people with power really go out of their way to use it.

It's not really going out of your way... I write my fair share of E-mail, or online chat, or digital documents... but when we leave PostIts on each other's desks, or send each other letters/messages in inter-departmental envelopes, they're all handwritten.
